Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the NovaVolt Automotive Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question during this time, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, please press star then two. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Chen, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Chen:
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to NovaVolt Automotive's Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Elena Vasquez, CEO; Michael Thornton, CFO; Raj Patel, Chief Manufacturing Officer; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Elena Vasquez.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q3 2024 was a strong quarter for NovaVolt Automotive. We made significant progress in several key areas, including navigating the impact of raw material costs and supply chain disruptions, accelerating growth in our energy business revenue and profitability, providing clear delivery volume guidance by model, advancing factory expansions and operational efficiency improvements, and outlining our capital expenditure plans and investment priorities. The demand for our VoltMax SUV continues to be strong, and we are working diligently to increase production capacity to meet that demand. The impact of this product lineup is exceeding our initial expectations, driving market share gains in key regions.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Thornton to discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Michael Thornton:
Thank you, Elena. Good morning, everyone. For Q3 2024, our revenue was $12.5 billion, representing a 52% increase year-over-year. Our gross margin was 23.1%, reflecting our ongoing efforts to improve operational efficiency amid challenging inputs. Our operating expenses were $2.1 billion, and net income was $1.4 billion. We continue to maintain a healthy balance sheet with $18.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents. Our guidance for the next quarter is revenue of $14.5 to $15.5 billion, with continued margin expansion.

Before we open the floor to questions, I'd like to dive deeply into one of the most critical factors shaping our P&L this quarter: the impact of raw material costs and supply chain disruptions. As you know, in the EV sector, our bill of materials—or BOM—is heavily weighted toward battery metals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and graphite, alongside structural materials such as aluminum and high-strength steel. These inputs represent roughly 45% of our cost of goods sold, or COGS, for our VoltOne sedan and VoltMax SUV platforms. Let me break this down with the data, trends, and our strategic countermeasures.

First, on raw material costs. We've seen a volatile but overall moderating environment compared to the peaks of 2022. Lithium carbonate equivalent prices, which directly feed our NMC and LFP cathode production, averaged $14.50 per kg in Q3, down 68% from the $45/kg frenzy in late 2022 driven by post-pandemic demand surges and supply bottlenecks in Australia’s spodumene mines. However, intra-quarter spikes—up 15% in September due to restocking ahead of Chinese New Year—added about 2.2 percentage points to our battery cell costs. Nickel, critical for our high-energy-density 2170 and next-gen 4680-style cells supplied by partners like Panasonic and LG Energy Solution, hovered at $17,200 per metric ton, still 25% above pre-2022 levels amid Indonesia's ongoing export quotas and the lingering effects of the 2022 LME short squeeze.

Cobalt prices stabilized at $28,000 per ton, benefiting from our shift toward lower-cobalt NMC 811 chemistries, while graphite anode material from China rose 12% YoY to $8,500 per ton due to anti-dumping probes in the EU. Aluminum, key for our gigacast body-in-white structures inspired by Tesla's Giga Press tech, climbed 8% to $2,600 per ton on energy surcharges from smelters in the Nordics. Aggregating this, raw material inflation drove a 9.8% YoY increase in our battery pack BOM, pushing average pack costs from $132/kWh in Q3 2023 to $139/kWh this quarter—still well below the $160/kWh industry benchmark from BloombergNEF.

This translated to a 6.4% headwind on gross margins, shaving 180 basis points off our adjusted automotive gross margin to 21.3%. Without mitigations—which I'll detail shortly—this could have been double that. For context, peers like Rivian reported similar 200 bps pressure in their Q2 call, while legacy players like Ford's Model e division cited 10-12% COGS inflation from EV-specific mats.

Now, shifting to supply chain disruptions, which compounded these cost pressures with volume hits. Geopolitical flashpoints were the culprits: Houthi attacks in the Red Sea forced 40% of our Asia-Europe container traffic to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope, adding 18-25 days to lead times from CATL's Ningde plants for our LFP packs. This delayed 12,000 units of VoltMax production in our Georgia Gigafactory, contributing to a 4.2% shortfall against our 85,000-unit quarterly guidance. Separately, the Panama Canal drought—exacerbated by El Niño—capped transits at 24 per day versus a normal 38, inflating freight costs by 22% for lithium hydroxide shipments from SQM in Chile to our Reno cell facility.

Semiconductor constraints lingered too, with automotive-grade chips from TSMC up 7% in allocation priority due to AI demand spillover—echoing the 2021 crunch but milder. Regionally, this hit us hardest in North America: our U.S. content for IRA compliance is now at 65% for the VoltOne, qualifying for the full $7,500 tax credit, but Asian-sourced black mass recycling inputs faced 30% longer ETAs. In Europe, where we're ramping Berlin deliveries, EU CBAM tariffs on carbon-intensive steel added $45 per vehicle, while China's dominance—supplying 75% of global refined lithium—exposed us to U.S. tariff risks under Section 301 reviews.

Our technical initiatives and strategic responses have been pivotal in clawing back control. On the cost side, we've locked in 60% of 2025 lithium needs via multi-year offtake agreements with Albemarle and Allkem at $12-14/kg floors, hedging 80% of Q4 exposure through LME futures—saving an estimated $120 million annualized. We're accelerating vertical integration: our Nevada cathode plant, using PVD-coated precursors à la Tesla's dry electrode process, hit 20 GWh capacity in Q3, cutting third-party cell reliance by 25% and stabilizing NMC costs at $85/kWh module-level.

We've qualified LFP cells from BYD and CATL for 40% of our packs, reducing nickel exposure by 35% and dropping energy density trade-offs to under 5% versus NMC—critical as LFP now comprises 55% of global EV sales per Rho Motion data. Recycling is ramping: our Redwood Materials partnership recovered 92% of lithium and 95% of nickel from Q3 teardowns, with black mass processing yielding material at 40% below spot—scaling to 50,000 tons/year by 2025.

Supply chain-wise, we're diversifying: dual-sourcing nickel from BHP in Australia and Tsingshan in Indonesia, with inventory buffers now at 90 days versus 60 pre-Q1. Freight-wise, airlifting high-value graphite from Syrah Resources in Mozambique offset Red Sea delays for $18 million, while our 'China-plus-one' strategy shifts 15% of anode production to India via Reliance's new Jamnagar hub. Digitally, our SAP-integrated S&OP platform with AI forecasting from Palantir cut disruption variance by 28%.

Looking forward, we expect raw material costs to trough in H1 2025 as new supply ramps—think Sigma Lithium's Phase 2 in Brazil adding 270ktpa LCE, and Indonesia's HPAL projects flooding nickel. BloombergNEF projects pack costs below $100/kWh by 2026, aligning with our $95/kWh target via solid-state R&D with QuantumScape. Disruptions should ease with Red Sea de-escalation and Panama rains, but we're stress-testing for 10% further freight hikes. Net-net, these headwinds cost us $285 million in Q3 EBITDA—5.2% of revenue—but our actions limited the margin hit to 180 bps, positioning us for 1,500 bps expansion to 25%+ gross margins at scale by 2026.

This resilience underscores our 'Fortress Supply Chain' thesis: derisked, localized, and tech-enabled. We're not just weathering the storm; we're emerging stronger than peers overly exposed to spot markets.

I'll now turn to our Energy generation and storage business, which once again delivered exceptional results this quarter, underscoring its role as a cornerstone of our long-term growth strategy in the EV and clean energy ecosystem. As you know, our Energy segment—encompassing large-scale Megapack utility projects, Powerwall residential and commercial storage, Solar Roof and panels, and our Autobidder AI-driven energy management software—is vertically integrated with our automotive vertical through shared 4680 cell production, manufacturing scale, and software stack. This synergy allows us to deploy gigawatt-hour scale energy solutions at costs that are 20-30% below industry averages, positioning us ahead of competitors like Fluence, NextEra Energy Resources, and CATL in the global BESS market.

Starting with the top line: Q3 Energy revenue came in at $2.8 billion, representing 162% year-over-year growth and 28% sequential growth from Q2. This marks our 12th straight quarter of triple-digit YoY growth, driven by record deployments and a burgeoning project backlog. Year-to-date, Energy revenue has reached $7.2 billion, now accounting for 22% of our total company revenue—up from just 8% two years ago. Breaking it down by product line:

Megapack utility-scale storage generated $1.9 billion (68% of segment revenue), up 195% YoY, fueled by 3.2 GWh of deployments—a new quarterly record, surpassing our prior high from Q1 by 25%. Key wins included the 1.5 GWh Phase 2 expansion of the Moss Landing project in California, rivaling Tesla's own record-scale site, and a 800 MWh deal with Pacific Gas & Electric for frequency regulation services.

Powerwall and Powerpack commercial/residential contributed $750 million (27%), with 1.1 GWh deployed, up 120% YoY. Virtual Power Plant (VPP) participation hit 150,000 units globally, aggregating over 500 MW of dispatchable capacity—think California's SGIP rebates and TEPA programs, where our Powerwall 3 units are now qualifying for 100% rebate coverage at $1,100/kWh installed.

Solar and services rounded out at $150 million (5%), with Solar Roof deployments accelerating 80% YoY as we ramped Austin Gigafactory production to 2 GW annualized run-rate.

Profitability remains our standout story. Segment gross margin expanded to 29.5% in Q3—up 950 basis points YoY and 400 bps sequentially—reflecting the benefits of our Shanghai Megafactory ramp, now at 40 GWh annual capacity (up from 20 GWh last year), and LTM-6 4680 cell costs dropping to $52/kWh, a 15% reduction QoQ thanks to dry electrode coating and structural pack innovations. This puts our levelized cost of storage (LCOS) at under $0.08/kWh for a 4-hour Megapack, 25% below the BloombergNEF global average. Operating expenses scaled efficiently at 8% of revenue, delivering EBITDA of $850 million—42% margin, more than double last year's figure. Excluding one-time Shanghai fab startup costs, adjusted EBITDA margin hit 46%, on par with pure-play leaders like Enphase but with vastly higher volume leverage.

Regionally, performance was robust across the board: North America (65% of revenue): Led by U.S. IRA-driven demand, with Megapack bookings up 220% YoY. California's NEM 3.0 transition has supercharged Powerwall adoption, with VPP curtailment revenue sharing yielding $50/unit annualized for participants—we've captured 35% market share here, ahead of Sonnen and Enphase.

Europe (20%): 140% YoY growth amid grid congestion from offshore wind intermittency. Highlights include a 500 MWh Berlin BESS for 50Hertz grid services and UK National Grid contracts leveraging our 15-year, 70% capacity warranty. EU CBAM tariffs are funneling hyperscalers like Google and Microsoft toward our U.S.-made packs.

Asia-Pacific (12%): Shanghai fab localization drove 300% YoY surge, with 1 GWh deployed in Australia (echoing our Hornsdale-esque Waratah Super Battery) and initial China traction via partnerships with State Grid. China’s 'Dual Carbon' goals position us for 10 GWh+ annual deployments by FY26.

Rest of World (3%): Emerging pilots in India and Brazil for rooftop solar + storage microgrids.

Strategically, we're doubling down on high-margin adjacencies. Autobidder V2.0, our AI frequency regulation platform, generated $120 million in ancillary services revenue—up 250% YoY—by optimizing 85% of global deployments for ISO/RTO markets like ERCOT and PJM. We've launched Megapack 3.0 with 3.9 MWh per unit (up 50% density), 4-hour duration, and liquid cooling for 60°C ambient ops, targeting data center backup amid AI GPU boom (think 100 MW pilots with NVDA hyperscalers). Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) integration is progressing, with 2025 Cybercab fleets enabling bidirectional charging for grid arbitrage—piloted in Norway with 95% round-trip efficiency.

Looking ahead, our Energy backlog stands at $12.5 billion (up 40% QoQ), with 75% contracted through 2026. We expect Q4 revenue of $3.2-3.5 billion (150%+ YoY) and full-year FY24 Energy revenue of $11-12 billion. Margins should hold at 28-30%, with Shanghai L4 ramp to 80 GWh by mid-2025 unlocking further scale. Energy isn't just diversification; it's our highest-ROIC business at 45% IRR on deployed capital, insulating us from auto cyclicality while fueling the EV megatrend.

As we wrap up what has been a transformative Q3 for NovaVolt Automotive, I'd like to dive into our delivery volume guidance by model, providing the granularity our investors have come to expect. Before I do, a quick reminder that all forward-looking statements are subject to the risks outlined in our SEC filings, including supply chain volatility, regulatory changes, and macroeconomic headwinds like elevated interest rates impacting auto financing.

First, let's contextualize Q3 actuals against our prior guidance. We delivered a record 185,000 vehicles globally, up 28% year-over-year (YoY) and 12% quarter-over-quarter (QoQ). This beat our guided range of 170,000 to 180,000 units, driven by stronger-than-expected demand for our VoltMax SUV lineup and improved Shanghai Gigafactory utilization, which hit 95% in September. Model-wise, VoltOne sedans accounted for 42% of mix at 78,000 units (+15% YoY), VoltMax SUVs at 52% or 96,000 units (+42% YoY, fueled by the refreshed Long Range AWD variant), and early VoltHaul pickups at 6% or 11,000 units from our Texas GigaTexas ramp.

Average Selling Price (ASP) held resilient at $48,200, down just 3% QoQ due to targeted incentives in Europe amid softening sedan demand, offset by premium trims and FSD-equivalent Nova Autonomy software uptake at 65% attach rate, adding ~$8,000 per vehicle in high-margin recurring revenue potential.

Now, turning to Q4 guidance and FY24 outlook. We're guiding Q4 deliveries to 210,000 to 220,000 units, implying 14-19% QoQ growth and positioning us for a 1.05 million full-year total, up 32% from FY23's 795,000. This assumes continued production scaling, with Berlin Gigafactory reaching 85% utilization by quarter-end on the back of our 4680 cell transition, which reduces costs by 15% per kWh and boosts energy density to 280 Wh/kg—critical for extending VoltMax range to 520 EPA miles.

Breaking it down by model:

VoltOne (Entry-Level Sedan): Q4 guidance of 75,000 to 80,000 units (36-38% of mix). We're tempering growth here to +8% YoY after lapping last year's surge, as sedan market share erodes to 25% globally amid SUV crossover preferences—think Tesla Model 3/Y dynamics but amplified by BYD's Seagull flooding China at sub-$10k pricing. Regionally, US deliveries flat at ~20,000 amid IRA tax credit clawbacks for non-North American content; China up 5% to 35,000 via price adjustments to ¥189,900 (~$26,500); Europe down 10% to 20,000 due to WLTP homologation delays on our next-gen LFP battery pack. Strategically, we're prioritizing inventory drawdown to 15 days' supply by year-end, redirecting CapEx to autonomy hardware retrofits that enable Level 3 certification in 2025.

VoltMax (Mid-Size SUV/Crossover): Our growth engine, guiding 115,000 to 120,000 units (55% of mix), +35% YoY. This reflects pent-up demand post our July performance variant launch with 1,020 hp tri-motor setup and 2.9s 0-60, rivaling Lucid Air Sapphire benchmarks. US leads at 50,000 units (+45% YoY), bolstered by $7,500 IRA point-of-sale rebates and fleet wins with Hertz-like partners; China at 45,000 (+30% YoY) despite 25% tariff headwinds, thanks to local sourcing of CATL Qilin cells hitting 1,000+ km CLTC range; Europe at 20,000 (+20% YoY) with EU Green Deal subsidies. Key initiative: 48V architecture rollout cuts BoM costs 12% while enabling OTA-upgradable ADAS, pushing Nova Autonomy take rate to 75%. We're on track for 600,000+ annual capacity at GigaTexas by Q1'25.

VoltHaul (Full-Size Pickup): Q4 ramp to 20,000 to 22,000 units (9-10% of mix), +150% YoY from Q3. Production hit 1,200/week in October at 92% OEE, leveraging structural battery packs for 500-mile range and 11,000 lb towing—directly challenging Rivian R1T and Ford F-150 Lightning. US-centric at 18,000 units, with 40% gross margins from $95,000+ ASPs; initial Europe exports minimal pending right-hand-drive certification. Headwinds include semiconductor shortages, but we've mitigated via TSMC diversification. FY24 total: 45,000 units, scaling to 100,000 in FY25 with Frunk expansion.

Emerging: VoltMini (Sub-$25k Compact EV): First deliveries Q4 at 1,000 units for validation, full ramp H1'25 targeting 150,000 annually from our new Thailand plant—strategic to counter BYD's $9,500 Seagull and VW's ID.2all in mass-market affordability wars. Features structural aluminum chassis and 60 kWh NMC pouch cells for 300-mile range at 3.5 mi/kWh efficiency.

Regionally, US at 45% of Q4 mix (up from 40% in Q3) on strong consumer sentiment and leasing penetration at 28%; China steady at 35% despite 8.7% NEV penetration saturation and price wars eroding industry ASPs 15% YoY; Europe at 18% (down from 22%) pressured by 2035 ICE ban uncertainties and German subsidy cuts, though UK ZEV mandate credits provide tailwinds; Rest of World (RoW) at 2%, growing via Mexico JV for NAFTA optimization.

Strategically, this guidance embeds resilience against headwinds: We've idled 10% of VoltOne lines temporarily to retool for 800V architecture, accelerating DC fast-charging to 350 kW and cutting charge times 30%. Gross margins expand to 21.5% in Q4 (from 19.8% Q3) via vertical integration—80% in-house batteries by FY25—and regulatory credits totaling $450M FY24. Risks include Cybertruck-like recall potential on VoltHaul steer-by-wire, but our 99.9% uptime on Dojo supercomputers for FSD validation de-risks that.

We're confident this positions NovaVolt for 1.5M+ deliveries in FY25, capturing share in the $7T addressable EV market by 2030 per BloombergNEF.

As we dive into our Q3 results, I'd like to spend some time on one of our key growth levers: factory expansions and operational efficiency improvements. These initiatives are central to our strategy at NovaVolt Automotive to scale production amid surging EV demand while driving down costs to protect and expand our industry-leading margins. In a market where global EV sales grew 28% year-over-year to over 14 million units—fueled by policy tailwinds like the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and Europe's Fit for 55 package—we're positioning ourselves not just to meet demand but to outpace it.

Let me start with factory expansions. We've invested aggressively in our global manufacturing footprint to boost annual vehicle output from 450,000 units today to over 1.2 million by end-2026. This includes $3.2 billion in capital expenditures this year alone, up 15% from our initial guidance, reflecting accelerated timelines driven by stronger-than-expected orders for our VoltMax SUV and VoltHaul platforms.

Our flagship move is the Phase 2 expansion of our Nevada Gigafactory, our North American hub modeled after Tesla's successful playbook but with a heavier emphasis on structural battery packs. We're adding 40 GWh of annual battery cell capacity—doubling our current 20 GWh—using our proprietary NMC-811 chemistry cells, which deliver 15% higher energy density than standard LFP packs. Construction is 75% complete, with first output ramping in Q2 2025. This will support IRA-compliant production, qualifying us for up to $7,500 per vehicle in consumer tax credits and $45/kWh in battery production credits, which we expect to flow through at a blended 12% margin uplift.

Complementing this, we're breaking ground next month on a $1.8 billion greenfield Gigafactory in Monterrey, Mexico—our "Gigafactory Mexico"—leveraging nearshoring benefits under USMCA. This 600,000 sqm facility will produce 300,000 vehicles annually, starting with our affordable VoltMini hatchback priced under $30,000 post-credits. Mexico's lower labor costs—about 25% below U.S. levels—and proximity to our U.S. supply chain will shave $1,200 per vehicle in logistics expenses. We're already securing lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) cells from CATL partnerships, mirroring BYD's vertical integration strategy, to mitigate raw material volatility amid lithium prices fluctuating 20% quarter-over-quarter.

In Europe, regulatory pressures from the EU's 2035 ICE ban have accelerated our Berlin-Brandenburg plant expansion by six months. We're investing €950 million to add 150,000 units of capacity, focusing on our Euro-6 compliant VoltOne Wagon with a 500 km WLTP range. This site now runs on 85% renewable energy, aligning with ESG mandates and reducing our Scope 2 emissions by 40% YoY. Asia remains a growth vector too: our joint venture with a major Indian OEM in Tamil Nadu is on track for 100,000 units in 2025, tapping into India's PLI scheme subsidies and the world's fastest-growing EV market at 50% CAGR.

These expansions aren't just about volume; they're engineered for flexibility. Our factories incorporate modular assembly lines capable of 48-hour model switches, a nod to Rivian's agile manufacturing ethos, ensuring we can pivot from sedans to pickups as U.S. truck demand—now 35% of EV sales—continues to outstrip sedans.

Turning to operational efficiency improvements, this is where we're truly differentiating. In Q3, we achieved a 22% reduction in cost of goods sold (COGS) per vehicle, bringing it to $28,500 from $36,600 a year ago—well ahead of the industry average of 18% cuts reported by peers like Ford and GM. This was driven by a multifaceted program we call "VoltStream," targeting Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) above 92%, up from 81% in 2023.

Key technical initiatives include AI-driven predictive maintenance across our lines. Using machine learning algorithms trained on 2.5 million hours of operational data, we've cut unplanned downtime by 35%, from 8% to 5.2% of runtime. This mirrors Tesla's Dojo supercomputer optimizations but leverages our partnership with Siemens for edge AI, reducing sensor costs by 40%.

We've also rolled out next-gen automation: 450 collaborative robots (cobots) from ABB and Fanuc handling 65% of welding and 50% of battery assembly tasks. This has improved first-pass yield on battery modules to 98.5%—a 12-point jump—slashing scrap rates and rework costs by $450 per pack. Our structural battery packs, akin to Tesla's 4680 but with silicon-doped anodes for 20% faster charging, now achieve 15-minute cycle times, enabling 48 vehicles per line per shift.

Supply chain resilience is another pillar. Vertical integration now covers 70% of our battery materials, including in-house cathode precursor production in Nevada using hydrothermal synthesis to bypass 30% of imported black mass. We've diversified nickel sourcing to Indonesia and Australia, hedging against the 15% price spike seen in Q3, and implemented a just-in-time (JIT) kanban system that reduced inventory turns from 12 to 18 per year.

Regionally, these efficiencies shine brightest in North America, where IRA localization has dropped our effective battery COGS to $85/kWh—competitive with LG Energy's $90/kWh benchmarks. In Europe, tariff optimizations and local sourcing have improved EBITDA margins by 4 points to 18%. Challenges persist in China, where intense competition from BYD's Blade batteries pressures pricing, but our Shanghai line's 25% throughput gains via digital twins—virtual factory simulations—keep us at 95% utilization.

Strategically, these efforts position NovaVolt for sustainable profitability in a margin-compressed EV landscape. Peers like Lucid and Fisker have struggled with capex overruns, but our 1.8x return on incremental capex—versus the industry's 1.2x—stems from disciplined phasing: 60% of expansions funded via operating cash flow, with the balance from green bonds at 4.2% yields. Looking ahead, we guide for $2.5 billion in efficiency savings over 2025-2027, fueling R&D into solid-state batteries and 800V architectures.

In summary, our factory expansions and efficiency gains aren't reactive; they're a blueprint for scaling to 20% U.S. EV market share by 2028 while delivering 25%+ gross margins.

Good afternoon, everyone. As we navigate a dynamic EV landscape marked by moderating demand growth in mature markets, intensifying competition from players like BYD and Tesla, and supportive tailwinds from the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and EU's Net-Zero Industry Act, our capital expenditure—or CapEx—strategy remains laser-focused on three pillars: scaling production capacity for profitability at volume, accelerating next-generation technology leadership, and fortifying supply chain resilience amid geopolitical tensions.

Let me dive into the numbers. For fiscal year 2024, we are guiding to total CapEx of $9.2 billion, up 18% from $7.8 billion in 2023, reflecting our commitment to outpacing industry capacity utilization trends, which currently hover around 65-70% globally per IHS Markit data. This represents about 22% of our projected revenue, in line with peers like Rivian at 25% and legacy OEMs like Ford targeting 15-20% for their EV ramps. Looking ahead, we expect FY2025 CapEx to rise to $11.5 billion to $12.8 billion, with a CAGR of 25% through 2027, funding our goal of reaching 2.5 million annual vehicle production capacity by 2028—doubling our current 1.2 million run rate.

Here's the breakdown by priority area, which we've optimized using our proprietary capacity planning model that factors in cell-to-pack efficiencies, gigacasting throughput, and regional incentive capture:

1. Manufacturing Expansion and Vertical Integration (55% of 2024 CapEx, or $5.1 billion)  
Our top priority is derisking supply chains and achieving cost leadership through localization. We're investing $2.8 billion in NovaGigafactory Texas Phase 2, which will add 500 GWh of annual battery pack assembly capacity by mid-2026, leveraging the IRA's full $7,500 per vehicle credit for North American-sourced content. This mirrors Tesla's Texas ramp but with a twist: 80% of output dedicated to our upcoming $28,000 'VoltPulse' compact crossover, targeting the mass-market segment where EV penetration is lagging at 12% in the U.S. per Cox Automotive.

In Europe, $1.2 billion goes to our Berlin-Brandenburg plant expansion, adding 300,000 units of structural battery pack integration for our VoltOne sedan, compliant with the EU Battery Regulation's 16% recycled content mandate by 2030. We're prioritizing gigacasting here too—scaling from 6,000-ton Giga Press to 9,000-ton units from IDRA, reducing body-in-white costs by 25% versus traditional stamping.

Regionally, Asia-Pacific gets $900 million for a new joint venture cathode plant in South Korea with Posco Future M, producing high-nickel NCM 811 precursors. This hedges against China's 100%+ dominance in refining, where LME cobalt prices have surged 40% YTD amid DRC export curbs. Mexico remains a wildcard: $200 million allocated for maquiladora tooling, eyeing USMCA benefits as tariffs loom on Chinese LFP cells.

2. Battery Technology and Powertrain Innovation (25% of CapEx, or $2.3 billion)  
Battery costs must drop below $60/kWh to hit sub-$100/kWh pack economics for affordable EVs. We're allocating $1.5 billion to qualify our in-house 46-series cylindrical cells—building on 4680 architecture—with silicon-doped anodes targeting 20% higher energy density than current LFP packs from CATL. Pilot lines in Shanghai are yielding 95% first-pass yield, with full scale-up in 2025.

A key initiative: $500 million for solid-state battery R&D, partnering with QuantumScape on sulfide-based electrolytes aiming for 500 Wh/kg by 2027—critical as competitors like Toyota tease 1,000 km range prototypes. We're also ramping dry electrode coating tech, licensed from Tesla's IP portfolio, to slash manufacturing CapEx per GWh by 30%. In parallel, $300 million funds bidirectional charging hardware for V2G/V2H, positioning us for California's 35% LDV electrification mandate by 2026.

3. Autonomy, Software, and Ecosystem Buildout (15% of CapEx, or $1.4 billion)  
Autonomy is our moat. $800 million accelerates Level 4 hardware-in-loop testing for NovaPilot Full Self-Driving (FSD) beta, with 10^9 mile Dojo-equivalent compute clusters training on edge-case data from our 1.5 million fleet. This supports robotaxi ambitions, where ARK Invest projects $10 trillion TAM by 2030.

$400 million builds out 50,000 DC fast chargers via our NovaCharge network, focusing on highway corridors in the U.S. Northeast and German Autobahn, capturing 15% utilization premiums per Electrify America benchmarks. Software-defined vehicle investments, including OTA updates for our NVOS 3.0 infotainment stack, round out the bucket.

4. Sustainability and Other (5% of CapEx, or $460 million)  
This funds water recycling at 95% efficiency in drought-prone Nevada and Scope 3 emissions tracking for EU CSRD compliance.

Strategic Insights and Risk Mitigation  
Our CapEx is front-loaded toward high-ROI assets: payback periods average 2.8 years at 80% utilization, versus industry 4.2 years per BCG analysis. We're de-risking via $3 billion in supplier pre-payments to LG Energy Solution and SK On, locking in 20 GWh at $80/kWh fixed pricing through 2027. Amid softening EU demand (EV sales down 11% YoY per ACEA), we're pivoting 20% of Berlin output to hybrids, blending CapEx flexibility.

In China, where we hold 3% market share, investments prioritize LFP for our 'VoltSpark' mini-SUV against BYD's Seagull, navigating 25% U.S. tariffs by routing via Mexico. Overall, this positions NovaVolt for 25% EBITDA margins by 2026, outpacing GM's EV unit losses and Tesla's 18% ASP compression.

We'll provide quarterly updates, but this CapEx blueprint drives our path to 15 million cumulative EVs by 2030.

I'll now turn the call over to Raj Patel to provide an update on our manufacturing operations.

Raj Patel:
Thank you, Michael. We are pleased with the progress we've made in scaling up production of VoltMax SUV. We are implementing several initiatives to further improve our manufacturing efficiency and reduce costs, including the VoltStream program and AI predictive maintenance, which have already delivered significant OEE gains. We are on track to meet our production targets for the year, with expansions in Nevada and Mexico set to unlock substantial additional capacity.

Now, I'll hand the call back to the operator for the Q&A session.

Operator:
